title: Alexander Pope
wiki_lead:
Alexander Pope (21 May 1688 O.S. – 30 May 1744) was an English poet, translator, and satirist of the Enlightenment era who is considered one of the most prominent English poets of the early 18th century. An exponent of Augustan literature, he is best known for his satirical and discursive poetry, including An Essay on Criticism (1711), The Rape of the Lock (1712–1717), The Dunciad (1728–1743), and for his translations of Homer.
Pope is often quoted in The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, some of his verses having entered common parlance (e.g. "damning with faint praise" or "to err is human; to forgive, divine").

Life
Alexander Pope was born in London on 21 May 1688, the year of the Glorious Revolution. His father, also Alexander Pope, was a successful linen merchant in the Strand, London. His mother was Edith Turner, a daughter of William Turner, Esquire, of York. Both were Catholic. His uncle-in-law was the miniature painter Samuel Cooper, through his mother's sister, Christiana. Pope's education was affected by the Test Acts, a set of English penal laws that upheld the status of the established Church of England, banning Catholics from teaching, attending a university, voting, or holding public office on penalty of perpetual imprisonment. Pope was taught to read by his aunt and attended Twyford School circa 1698. He also attended two Roman Catholic schools in London. Such schools, though illegal, were tolerated in some areas.

In 1700 his family moved to a small estate at Popeswood, in Binfield, Berkshire, close to the royal Windsor Forest. This was due to strong anti-Catholic sentiment and a statute preventing "Papists" from living within 10 miles (16 km) of London or Westminster. Pope later described the countryside around the house in his poem "Windsor-Forest". Pope's formal education then ended, and he thereafter mostly educated himself by reading the works of classical writers such as the satirists Horace and Juvenal, the epic poets Homer and Virgil, and English authors such as Geoffrey Chaucer, William Shakespeare and John Dryden. He studied many languages, reading French, Italian, Latin, and Greek poets. After five years of study, Pope came into contact with figures from London literary society such as William Congreve, Samuel Garth and William Trumbull.
Pope is popularly believed to have composed his early poems beneath a beech tree in a grove half a mile from his house in Binfield. This tree was later carved with the words "Here Pope sung" and became a tourist destination termed "Pope's Tree". By the 1820s, numerous visitors had carved their names and dates of visiting on the tree. Pope's Tree had reportedly become visibly aged and lost most of its canopy by this point.
At Binfield Pope made many important friends. One of them, John Caryll the younger (the future dedicatee of The Rape of the Lock), was 20 years older than Pope and had made many acquaintances in the London literary world. He introduced Pope to the ageing playwright William Wycherley and to William Walsh, a minor poet, who helped Pope revise his first major work, The Pastorals. In 1707 Pope met the Blount sisters, Teresa and Martha (Patty). He remained close friends with Patty until his death, but his friendship with Teresa ended in 1722.

From the age of 12 Pope suffered many health problems, including Pott disease, a form of tuberculosis that affects the spine, which deformed his body and stunted his growth, leaving him with a severe hunchback. His tuberculosis caused other health problems, including respiratory difficulties, high fevers, inflamed eyes and abdominal pain. He grew to a height of only 4 feet 6 inches (1.37 metres). Pope was already removed from society as a Catholic, and his poor health alienated him further. Though he never married, he had many female friends to whom he wrote witty letters, including Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, and it has been speculated that Martha Blount was his lover. Born in London to Roman Catholic parents amid anti-Catholic restrictions that barred him from formal universities, Pope was largely self-educated and overcame chronic health issuesâincluding a spinal deformity from Pott's disease that stunted his growth to about four feet six inches and caused lifelong painâto produce enduring works such as An Essay on Criticism (1711), the mock-epic The Rape of the Lock (1712â1714), and his translation of Homer's Iliad (1715â1720). Pope's poetry emphasized neoclassical ideals of order, wit, and moral instruction, influencing generations of writers through pieces like An Essay on Man (1733â1734), which philosophically reconciled human limitations with divine providence, and The Dunciad (1728â1743), a scathing satire targeting literary dunces and cultural decline. His achievements included financial independence from writing, rare for poets of his era, achieved via subscriptions for his Homer translations and villa in Twickenham, where he cultivated a celebrated garden. Yet, Pope's sharp tongue sparked controversies, including bitter feuds with critics like Lewis Theobald and publishers like Edmund Curll, whom he lampooned mercilessly, and accusations of personal malice in his satires that alienated former allies such as Joseph Addison. Despite physical frailties exploited by rivals to mock his appearance, Pope's intellectual vigor and stylistic precision cemented his legacy as one of England's most quoted poets.
